General Background

NAD+ and NADP+ are dinucleotides containing one nicotinamide base and one adenine base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety. Their oxidized forms are depicted here as NAD+ and NADP+ due to the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring. Their reduced forms are referred to as NADH and NADPH.

These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as cofactors. They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes".

The most common function of NAD+ is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts NAD+ to NADH, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form.

NADPH, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of NADP+, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms NADP+ is reduced by photosystem I. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see pentose phosphate pathway (oxidative branch) I).

Despite their importance, the regulation of NAD+ phosphorylation and dephosphorylation remains incompletely defined. Earlier work on the kinetics of pyridine nucleotide metabolism in Escherichia coli demonstrated that the ratio of NADP+ to NAD+ results largely from the rates of NADP+ and NAD+ interconversion (in [Lundquist73]).

In Escherichia coli the reversible reduction of both NAD+ and NADP+ is carried out by the two transhydrogenase isoforms shown in the reaction links. The PntAB complex, encoded by the pntA and pntB genes, is located in the inner membrane and also functions as a proton pump. Its physiological function is to catalyze energy-dependent reduction of NADP+ with NADH. The soluble product of gene sthA is thought to function mainly in the reoxidation of NADPH with NAD+. The expression of these two isoforms is modulated by the redox state of cellular metabolism [Sauer04]. In [Lundquist71] and reviewed by Penfound, T. and J.W. Foster in [Neidhardt96] (see below).

About This Pathway

NAD kinases have been characterized in organisms from a variety of taxonomic groups including archaea, eubacteria and eukaryotes (reviewed in [Kawai08]). The NAD kinase of Salmonella enterica has been shown to be essential for growth [Grose06] and evidence for its essentiality in Escherichia coli has been presented [Gerdes02].

In contrast, NADP phosphatases (NADPases) remain poorly characterized despite their important role. Although an NAD kinase homolog in the archaeon Methanocaldococcus jannaschii was shown to also have NADP phosphatase activity, NADP phosphatases from eubacterial and eukaryotic sources still require identification of the genes encoding them and further study of their enzymatic properties. In Escherichia coli the product of cysQ showed high NADP and NADPH phosphatase activities, but kinetic studies of the purified enzyme suggested that it is not the true NADP phosphatase of this organism. Reviewed in [Kawai08, Pollak07].

Reviewed in Penfound, T. and J.W. Foster (1996) "Biosynthesis and Recycling of NAD", chapter 48, pp. 721-730, in [Neidhardt96].

slots.text:
The enzyme is usually assayed with NADPH and thio-NAD+ as substrates, monitoring the reduction of thio-NAD+. The enzyme activity has also been measured with NADH and thio-NADP+ as substrates. Although it is annotated as a B-specific enzyme, it appears that the stereospecificity has not been experimentally determined [Boonstra99, Cao11, Partipilo22].

Activity is strongly inhibited by excess NADPH, but not thio-NAD+ [Cao11].

slots.text:
NAD kinase appears to be an allosteric enzyme, with activity tightly coupled to the NADPH/NADP+ and NADH/NAD+ ratios present in the cell. That suggests that NAD kinase may play an important role in the regulation of NADP turnover and size of the NADP pool [Zerez87, Kawai01].

nadK is likely essential for growth [Gerdes02, Baba06].

Site-directed mutagenesis studies of the E. coli enzyme showed that a R175G mutation relaxed the strict NAD substrate specificity of the enzyme, resulting in a low level of ATP-dependent NADH kinase activity [Mori05].

Structure-function relationships in NAD kinases from archaea, bacteria (including E. coli) and eukaryotes have been reviewed [Magni06, Kawai08, Shi09].

slots.text:
Alkaline phosphatase is a periplasmic, homodimeric enzyme that catalyses the hydrolysis and transphosphorylation of a wide variety of phosphate monoesters [Torriani60, Heppel62, Malamy61, Chang80]. The reaction proceeds through a phosphoseryl intermediate with the subsequent release of inorganic phosphate and alcohol [Schwartz61, Holtz99, Stec98, Stec00a]. The transphosphorylation reaction results in the transfer of a phosphoryl group to the alcohol of acceptors such as Tris or ethanolamine [Dayan64, Wilson64] . Alkaline phosphatase is a metalloenzyme, binding two zinc atoms and one magnesium ion per monomer [Plocke62, Plocke62a, Sowadski85, Janeway93].

The amount of alkaline phosphatase is optimal when cells are starved for phosphate - which is the most common environment for E. coli in the human gut - and is much reduced when there is an excess of phosphate [Torriani60]. Under conditions of limiting phosphate, alkaline phosphatase accounts for approximately 6% of the total protein synthesized [Garen60]

Alkaline phosphatase occurs in three major forms designated isozymes 1, 2 and 3 whose relative proportions are dependent on the growth conditions [Kelley73, Schlesinger68]. The isozymes are differentiated by the presence or absence of an NH2-terminal arginine residue: present in both subunits of isozyme 1, absent in both subunits of isozyme 3 and heterogenous in isozyme 2 [Nakata78, Bradshaw81]. Removal of the N-terminal arginine is catalysed by the membrane-associated, proteolytic enzyme Iap [Nakata77, Nakata84].

The precursor polypeptide is secreted across the inner membrane to the periplasmic space concommitant with removal of the signal sequence [Chang86a]. Folding of PhoA in vivo is catalysed by the periplasmic protein, DsbA and is thought to occur as the polypeptide elongates from the ribosome [Kadokura09].

phoA is part of the phosphate regulon; its expression is positively regulated by the PhoB transcriptional regulator [Makino86]

A recent report has also suggested that the PhoA protein oxidizes phosphite to phosphate, producing molecular H2 [Yang04a].

Reviews: [Coleman92, Holtz99, Stigbrand82, Torriani90]

slots.text:
PntAB is a membrane bound, proton translocating, pyridine nucleotide transhydrogenase which couples the reversible reduction of NADP+ by NADH to proton translocation across the membrane [Clarke85b, Clarke85a]. The activity of PntAB is a major source of cytosolic NADPH in E. coli [Sauer04].

The functional enzyme assembles as a tetramer composed of two α (PntA) and two β (PntB) subunits [Hou90a]. The enzyme complex contains three domains: domains I and III protrude from the membrane and contain the binding sites for NAD(H) and NADP(H) respectively [Johansson05b] and domain II which spans the membrane and contains the proton translocation pathway. The transmembrane domain consists of 13 α-helices (4 from the α subunit and 9 from the β subunit) [Meuller99].

E. coli also contains an energy independent soluble pyridine nucleotide transhydrogenase encoded by the sthA gene. Its primary physiological role appears to be the reoxidation of NADPH [Canonaco01, Sauer04]. The two transhydrogenases are also distinguished by the stereospecificity of the reducing equivalents transfer (see [You85]); PntAB is annotated as an AB (Re-Si)-specific transhydrogenase which acts on the pro-R hydrogen (or A hydrogen) of the nicotinamide ring of NADH [Hoek74] and the pro-S hydrogen (B hydrogen) of NADPH.

Reviews: [Rydstrom98, Bizouarn00, Jackson91a, Bizouarn02, Pedersen08, Jackson12b, Zhang17c]

slots.text:
pntA encodes the α subunit of membrane-bound proton-translocating pyridine nucleotide transhydrogenase.

The α subunit is predicted to consist of a large N-terminal cytosolic region (domain I) which binds NAD(H) [Fjellstrom95, Johansson05b], followed by 4 transmembrane regions and a short C-terminal tail [Clarke86, Tong91, Ahmad92a, Holmberg94, Glavas93].

slots.text:
pntB encodes the β subunit of membrane-bound proton-translocating pyridine nucleotide transhydrogenase.

The β subunit contains an N-terminal domain with 6 - 8 transmembrane regions and a cytosolic C-terminal domain that binds NADP(H) [Clarke86, Tong91, Ahmad92a, Holmberg94, Bragg97].

Early studies characterized the pnt-1 mutation (PntB G314E [Ahmad92]) which causes loss of both energy-dependent and energy-independent pyridine nucleotide transhydrogenase activity [Zahl78, Hanson79].

slots.text:
E. coli contains both a soluble and a membrane-bound pyridine nucleotide transhydrogenase. The soluble pyridine nucleotide transhydrogenase is the sthA gene product; its primary physiological role appears to be the reoxidation of NADPH [Canonaco01, Sauer04]. The membrane-bound proton-translocating transhydrogenase is the pntAB gene product; PntAB is a major source of NADPH [Sauer04].

SthA contains noncovalently bound FAD and is present in a form consisting of seven or eight monomers [Boonstra99].

Moderate overexpression of SthA allows an increased maximal growth rate of a phosphoglucose isomerase mutant [Canonaco01], and a pgi sthA double mutant is not viable [Sauer04]. These phenotypes may be due to the ability of SthA to restore the cellular redox balance under conditions of excess NADPH formation [Canonaco01, Sauer04]. Mutations in sthA appear during adaptation of a pgi mutant strain to growth on glucose minimal medium [Charusanti10].

Transcription of sthA is downregulated by growth on glycerol [Sauer04].

In E. coli mutant strains grown on different carbon sources, such as glycerol and glucose for an lrp mutant and glucose for an arcA mutant strain, the udhA promoter activity was increased, suggesting a role as a repressor for those regulators [Haverkorn16].

A NADH-consuming transhydrogenase activity was characterized as well as an uncoupling activity of NAD(P)H oxidase reaction that produces hydrogen peroxide and superoxide radical under aerobic conditions [Partipilo22].

slots.text:
IHF, "Integration host factor," is a global regulatory protein that helps to maintain DNA architecture. It binds and bends DNA at specific sites. IHF plays a role in DNA supercoiling and DNA duplex destabilization and affects processes such as DNA replication, recombination, and the expression of many genes [Swinger04, Freundlich92, Dhavan02].

To regulate DNA replication, IHF binds to three loci in DNA, named oriC (origin of replication), datA (prevents untimely replication initiations), and DARS2 (promotes exchange of ADP/ATP in DnaA protein) [Kasho21]. Before DNA replication initiation, IHF binds to the oriC region in a DnaA box R1-dependent manner and to the DARS2 region, and it is rapidly released from these sites after replication initiation to bind to other loci [Kasho21, Miyoshi21]|. There are two specific binding sites for IHF in the oriC region and two in the DARS2 region [Kasho21, Miyoshi21].

IHF is highly abundant in the cell. Its total intracellular concentration varies with growth rate and is higher in exponential phase, with 6,000 dimers per cell, than in stationary phase (3,000 dimers per cell) [Ali99].

IHF acts mostly as an accessory factor, stabilizing a correct nucleoprotein complex. For example, IHF was originally found to be required for the site-specific recombination of phage λ with the chromosome [Miller80a]. For this, IHF stabilizes the bending of the DNA to facilitate binding of the bivalent integrase molecules [Moitoso89]. There are two distinct DNA-bending steps during site recognition by IHF. The fast-phase step entails nonspecific DNA bending, while the slow phase involves specific DNA kinking during site recognition [Velmurugu18]. As another example, IHF stimulates transcription at σ54-dependent promoters. Here, IHF acts to facilitate the formation of the loop between the upstream bound activator and the σ54 holoenzyme [Hoover90, Santero92].

Like HU, IHF plays a role in polyamine-dependent DNA condensation. The binding to low-affinity sites and introduction of sharp bends in chromosomal DNA promote the formation of rod-like condensed structures in chromosomal DNA [Sarkar09].

The intrinsic curvature and flexibility of binding sites of IHF were investigated. The preference of IHF for intrinsically curved and flexible DNA suggest a positive role in bending the DNA, since genomic regions with higher curvature and flexibility are generally easy to bend [Liu18c]. The binding sites for IHF have high intrinsic curvature compared with flanking regions, and these are characterized by high structural flexibility [Liu18c].

IHF is a heterodimer consisting of two subunits, IhfA (HimA) and IhfB (HimD, Hip), that share about 25% amino acid identity [Nash87]. The structure of IHF bound to DNA has been solved [Rice96, Ellenberger97]. It binds tightly to DNA regions of about 40 bp carrying the 13-bp consensus sequence with A/T-rich elements upstream of the core consensus sequence [Goodrich90, Friedman88, Hales96]. IHF makes no contact with the major groove and only a few contacts with the minor groove [Yang89a]. Therefore, specificity is believed to be due to the sequence-dependent structural parameters of the DNA, where A/T-rich regions play an important role. The bend angle induced by IHF is approximately 160° [Rice96]. Multiple conformations of bent DNA bound to IHF have been determined [Connolly18, Purkait21, Yoshua21]. The three binding types of the DNA-IHF interaction form different angles of bending in DNA: associated, half-wrapped, and fully wrapped [Yoshua21]. In the first one, both sides of DNA interact with the protein binding DNA without wrapping (angle of 66o bend); in the second one an arm of the DNA wraps the protein (115o); in the third one the two arms of the DNA wrap IHF (157o) [Yoshua21]. It is worth mentioning that only with the DNA specific consensus sequence for IHF does the fully wrapped type occur [Yoshua21]. In addition, IHF appears to be able to bind to two DNA strands through a bridge using unspecific sequence [Yoshua21].

IHF is necessary for the induction of arginine- and lysine-dependent acid resistance (AR) via both transcriptional and translational controls of gene expression, as IHF activates expression of a specific set of genes involved in survival at extremely acidic pH [Bi14].

In cellular growth with succinate or pyruvate as a carbon source, IHF appears to be involved in persister cell formation through the regulation of expression of proteins related to the carbon flux [Nicolau22]. A knockout mutant for IHF enhances the level of ATP in the cell and diminishes persisters [Nicolau22].

An increase in MgCl2 concentration changesthe way IHF binds to DNA, from bending to folding. This interaction is notaffectedby pH or temperature changes [Lee15b].

A library of synthetic complex promoters was developed for the global regulators CRP and IHF; the promoters were formed by a weak 35/10 consensus sequence preceded by four combinatorial binding sites for these two TFs [Monteiro18]. CRP and IHF have very different regulatory effects: cis elements for CRP preferentially activate promoters when located immediately upstream of the promoter consensus, while binding sites for IHF mainly function as UP elements and transcription is stimulated in several different architectures in the absence of this protein [Monteiro18]. The extrapolation of these properties of complex synthetic promoters to naturally occurring regulatory systems could significantly impact the engineering of synthetic biological circuits in bacteria [Monteiro18].

A single-deletion mutants involving genes that encode IHF protein growing under anaerobic fermentation conditions caused decreased nucleotide synthesis, decreased glucose and ammonia uptake rates, and enhanced nitrogen transport and accumulation of amino acids and their precursors, as well as derepression of the aerobic TCA cycle and alternate carbon metabolic proteins [Iyer21]. The activities of some transcription factors appear to be enhanced (CysB, ArgR, PuuR) in fis gene mutants [Iyer21]. [Kargeti18] et al. reported a relative increase in the glucose uptake rate above that required for the observed growth rate. In addition, higher ATP synthesis and redox balance rates were reported relative to the observed growth rate and biomass yield in the mutant [Kargeti18].

Based on proteomic studies, it was determined that the activities of nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) such as H-NS, HU, IHF, and FIS are also modulated by posttranslational modifications (PTMs) that signal differences in growth conditions; because none of the NAPs are known to bind any signaling ligands, these growth condition signals may be compensated for by these PTMs [Dilweg18].

Based on synthetic promoter variants harboring consensus cis-elements, it was demonstrated that both Fis and IHF can recognize the consensus binding site of the other. However, changing this arrangement of the cis-elements can completely abolish the nonspecific binding of both. Combining cis-elements for both TFs could result in Fis and IHF repressed or activated promoters, depending on the final architecture of the promoters, in an unpredictable way [Monteiro20].

Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of IHF appears to increase [Deter21].

Reviews: [Dorman22]

<comment datatype="string">IHF, "<b>I</b>ntegration <b>h</b>ost <b>f</b>actor," is a global regulatory protein that helps to maintain DNA architecture. It binds and bends DNA at specific sites. IHF plays a role in DNA supercoiling and DNA duplex destabilization and affects processes such as DNA replication, recombination, and the expression of many genes [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15102446">Swinger04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1447969">Freundlich92</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11827473">Dhavan02</a>].
<p>
To regulate DNA replication, IHF binds to three loci in DNA, named oriC (origin of replication), datA (prevents untimely replication initiations), and DARS2 (promotes exchange of ADP/ATP in DnaA protein) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34475859">Kasho21</a>].   Before DNA replication initiation, IHF binds to the oriC region in a DnaA box R1-dependent manner and to the DARS2 region, and it is rapidly released from these sites after replication initiation to bind to other loci [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34475859">Kasho21</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34871419">Miyoshi21</a>]|. There are two specific binding sites for IHF in the oriC region and two in the DARS2 region  [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34475859">Kasho21</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34871419">Miyoshi21</a>].
<p>

IHF is highly abundant in the cell. Its total intracellular concentration varies with growth rate and is higher in exponential phase, with 6,000 dimers per cell, than in stationary phase (3,000 dimers per cell) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10515926">Ali99</a>].
<p>
IHF acts mostly as an accessory factor, stabilizing a correct nucleoprotein complex. For example, IHF was originally found to be required for the site-specific recombination of phage &lambda; with the chromosome [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6251971">Miller80a</a>]. For this, IHF stabilizes the bending of the DNA to facilitate binding of the bivalent integrase molecules [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2544029">Moitoso89</a>]. There are two distinct DNA-bending steps during site recognition by IHF. The fast-phase step entails nonspecific DNA bending, while the slow phase involves specific DNA kinking during site recognition [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29267885">Velmurugu18</a>]. As another example, IHF stimulates transcription at &sigma;<sup>54</sup>-dependent promoters. Here, IHF acts to facilitate the formation of the loop between the upstream bound activator and the &sigma;<sup>54</sup> holoenzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2208275">Hoover90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1404379">Santero92</a>]. 
<p>
Like HU, IHF plays a role in polyamine-dependent DNA condensation. The binding to low-affinity sites and introduction of sharp bends in chromosomal DNA promote the formation of rod-like condensed structures in chromosomal DNA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19132923">Sarkar09</a>]. 
<p>
The intrinsic curvature and flexibility of binding sites of IHF were investigated. The preference of IHF for intrinsically curved and flexible DNA suggest a positive role in bending the DNA, since genomic regions with higher curvature and flexibility are generally easy to bend [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29625128">Liu18c</a>]. The binding sites for IHF have high intrinsic curvature compared with flanking regions, and these are characterized by high structural flexibility  [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29625128">Liu18c</a>].
<p>
IHF is a heterodimer consisting of two subunits, IhfA (HimA) and IhfB (HimD, Hip), that share about 25% amino acid identity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3305480">Nash87</a>]. The structure of IHF bound to DNA has been solved [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8980235">Rice96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9032076">Ellenberger97</a>]. It binds tightly to DNA regions of about 40 bp carrying the 13-bp consensus sequence with A/T-rich elements upstream of the core consensus sequence [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2205834">Goodrich90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2972385">Friedman88</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8650000">Hales96</a>]. IHF makes no contact with the major groove and only a few contacts with the minor groove [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2541927">Yang89a</a>]. Therefore, specificity is believed to be due to the sequence-dependent structural parameters of the DNA, where A/T-rich regions play an important role. The bend angle induced by IHF is approximately 160&deg; [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8980235">Rice96</a>].  Multiple conformations of bent DNA bound to IHF have been determined [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30336035">Connolly18</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33418050">Purkait21</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34352078">Yoshua21</a>]. The three binding types of the DNA-IHF interaction form different angles of bending in DNA: associated, half-wrapped, and fully wrapped [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34352078">Yoshua21</a>]. In the first one, both sides of DNA interact with the protein binding DNA without wrapping (angle of 66<sup>o</sup> bend); in the second one an arm of the DNA wraps the protein (115<sup>o</sup>); in the third one the two arms of the DNA wrap IHF (157<sup>o</sup>) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34352078">Yoshua21</a>]. It is worth mentioning that only with the DNA specific consensus sequence for IHF does the fully wrapped type occur [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34352078">Yoshua21</a>].  In addition, IHF appears to be able to bind to two DNA strands through a bridge using unspecific sequence [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34352078">Yoshua21</a>].
<p>
IHF is necessary for the induction of arginine- and lysine-dependent acid resistance (AR) via both transcriptional and translational controls of gene expression, as IHF activates expression of a specific set of genes involved in survival at extremely acidic pH [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24816374">Bi14</a>]. 
<p>

<p>
An increase in MgCl<sub>2</sub> concentration changesthe way IHF binds to DNA, from bending to folding. This interaction is notaffectedby pH or temperature changes [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26657062">Lee15b</a>].

CRP and IHF have very different regulatory effects: <i>cis</i> elements for CRP preferentially activate promoters when located immediately upstream of the promoter consensus, while binding sites for IHF mainly function as UP elements and transcription is stimulated in several different architectures in the absence of this protein [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29091423">Monteiro18</a>]. The extrapolation of these properties of complex synthetic promoters to naturally occurring regulatory systems could significantly impact the engineering of synthetic biological circuits in bacteria [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29091423">Monteiro18</a>].
<p>
A single-deletion mutants involving genes that encode IHF protein growing under anaerobic fermentation conditions caused decreased nucleotide synthesis, decreased glucose and ammonia uptake rates, and enhanced nitrogen transport and accumulation of amino acids and their precursors, as well as derepression of the aerobic TCA cycle and alternate carbon metabolic proteins [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. The activities of some transcription factors appear to be enhanced (CysB, ArgR, PuuR) in fis gene mutants [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29748694">Kargeti18</a>] et al. reported a relative increase in the glucose uptake rate above that required for the observed growth rate. In addition, higher ATP synthesis and redox balance rates were reported relative to the observed growth rate and biomass yield in the mutant [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29748694">Kargeti18</a>].
<p>
Based on proteomic studies, it was determined that the activities of nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) such as  H-NS, HU, IHF, and FIS are also modulated by posttranslational modifications (PTMs) that signal differences in growth conditions; because none of the NAPs are known to bind any signaling ligands, these growth condition signals may be compensated for by these PTMs [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30287510">Dilweg18</a>].
<p>
Based on synthetic promoter variants harboring consensus cis-elements, it was demonstrated that both Fis and IHF can recognize the consensus binding site  of the other. However, changing this arrangement of the cis-elements can completely abolish the nonspecific binding of both. Combining cis-elements for both TFs could result in Fis and IHF repressed or activated promoters, depending on the final architecture of the promoters, in an unpredictable way [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32626694">Monteiro20</a>].
<p>
Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of IHF appears to increase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33731833">Deter21</a>].

slots.text:
The transcriptional dual regulator CRP, "cAMP receptor protein," also called CAP, "catabolite gene activator protein," regulates the expression of over 180 genes [Grainger05, Robison98, Zheng04] in E. coli. Many of these genes are involved in the catabolism of secondary carbon sources (for reviews, see [Fic09, Deutscher08, Gorke08, Kolb93]. In addition, CRP is involved in many other processes, such as osmoregulation [Landis99, Balsalobre06], stringent response [Johansson00], biofilm formation [Jackson02d], virulence [Balsalobre06], nitrogen assimilation [Mao07, Paul07a, Tian01a], iron uptake [Zhang05e], competence [Sinha09a], multidrug resistance to antibiotics [Nishino08a, Hirakawa06, Cho21a], cellular death processes caused by stress [Zeng22a], and expression of CyaR sRNA [De09]. Transcriptome analyses have been performed [Khankal09, GutierrezRios07, Zheng04, Gosset04]. Expression of crp is positively and negatively autoregulated [Aiba83, Hanamura92]; repression of crp requires Fis [GonzalezGil98]. CRP plays an important role in persistent cell formation [Uppal16], as has been shown by activation of a gene potentially related to persistence [Uppal14].

The activity of CRP on its targets indirectly reduces the expression of genes that are not CRP targets. This appears to happen because the regulation of CRP as a global regulator consumes the resources necessary for the expression of other genes, such as genes of anabolism [Kochanowski21].

CRP was the first purified transcriptional regulator and the first regulator for which the structure was solved [Zubay70, Emmer70, McKay81, Aiba82]. CRP is activated as a DNA-binding protein via binding of its allosteric effector, cAMP [Zubay70, McKay81, Blaszczyk01a]. The hydrogen-bonding abilities of the Thr127 and Ser128 residues at the cAMP pocket play a key role in stabilizing the CRP inactive form and in providing high cAMP affinity. However, these residues are not critical for cAMP-induced CRP activation [Gunasekara15]. The CRP lysine (K100) residue promotes CRP activity at class II promoters and helps to ensure proper CRP steady-state levels. On the other hand, acetylation of this residue is a mechanism by which the cell downregulates CRP-dependent class II promoter activity while elevating CRP steady-state levels, thus indirectly increasing class I promoter activity [Davis18a]. CRP K100 can be acetylated by acP in vitro and in vivo [Davis18a]. In minimal medium with glycerol, CRP is acetylated by the Nε-lysine acetyltransferase YfiQ; this effect is triggered by high levels of ppGpp, which promote yfiQ expression [Ro21]. CRP acetylation by YfiQ affects the activation promoters class I, while CRP acetylation in K100 by acetyl phosphate does not [Ro21]. The CRP residues acetylated by YfiQ are not yet known [Ro21].

cAMP-dependent catabolite repression plays a role in the regulation of biofilm growth in response to sugars [Sutrina15]. The metabolism of lactose, L-arabinose, and D-xylose is regulated in a hierarchical manner through cAMP, where lactose is clearly the preferred sugar, followed by L-arabinose and then D-xylose [Ammar18]. Microstates of CRP bound to cAMP have been analyzed by [Chkheidze20]. Based on semisynthetic promoters containing different lengths of the spacer relative to the TSS, as well as natural Class II promoters in the presence of wild-type (WT) CRP or K100 mutant CRP, it was determined that the expression profiles of these promoters at different distances from the CRP site were similar in both the K100 mutants and WT CRP, with the highest activity at the -41.5 length of the spacer relative to the TSS [EcijaConesa20]. It is proposed that CRP K100 acetylation is required for full promoter activity and could involve a fine-tuning of gene expression dynamics in the stress response [EcijaConesa20]. The K100 influence was dependent on the spacing (in base pairs) between the CRP binding site and the A2 of the 10 element; it was confirmed that the ideal CRP binding site for the gatY promoter is the same as that for the -41.5 semisynthetic promoter. The results could help in understanding why 34% of natural Class II CRP-dependent promoters are centered on -41.5 [EcijaConesa20].

Based on IR spectroscopy and computational analysis, the energy landscapes of WT and several mutated CRPs were defined to determine how a homodimeric protein can distinguish nonpalindromic DNA sequences and facilitate communication between residues located in three different activation regions (AR) for class II CRP-dependent promoters [Evangelista19].

In addition to the role as a transcription factor, a role for CRP as a Nucleoid-associated protein (NAP) has been proposed, because a global effect of this TF in gene expression and a positive effect on DNA positive supercoiling state have been observed with its apo conformation (CRP without cAMP) [Heyde21].

On the other hand, the loss of cAMP is compensated by a mutant in the DNA topoisomerase TopA, a protein that relaxes negatively supercoiled DNA, suggesting the importance of the supercoiling status of promoters regulated by CRP [Heyde21].

Protein structure and allosteric activation

CRP belongs to the CRP-FNR superfamily of transcription factors [Korner03, Green01]. The crystal structures of cAMP-CRP [McKay82, Weber87, Passner00], cAMP-CRP bound to DNA [Schultz91a, Parkinson96, Passner97, Huang13a], the cAMP-CRP-α-CTD-DNA complex [Benoff02], and the solution structure [Popovych09], as well as the crystal structure of apo-CRP [Sharma09b], have been solved. CRP is a homodimer and consists of two domains connected by a short hinge region. The C-terminal α-helical DNA-binding domain carries a characteristic helix-turn-helix motif. It dimerizes in apo-CRP, with the DNA recognition helix F buried within its core [Sharma09b]. The N-terminal dimerization domain mainly consists of β-sheets and carries a hydrophobic pocket for binding of cAMP. A long α-helix, termed the C-helix, forms an intersubunit coiled-coil. This helix plays a central role in the allosteric activation of CRP. Allostery arises as a natural consequence of changes in global low-frequency protein fluctuations on ligand binding, and there are conserved residues crucial for allosteric control [Rodgers13]. After binding of cAMP, the CRP signal is propagated through lengthening and reorientation of the C-helix to the DNA-binding domain, resulting in the liberation of the DNA recognition helix [Popovych09, Sharma09b]. The CRP C-terminal DNA-binding domain (CDD) is capable of forming a dimer in solution, and this conformation may be involved in cAMP-induced allosteric activation of CRP [Sim17].

At different pH values, the thermodynamics of cAMP binding to CRP and the transmission of signal inside CRP that goes from cAMP binding to DNA binding have been described [Evangelista21]. The transmission of signal involves changes in stability, connectivity, and the interaction affinity of internal components of the CRP dimer, such as residues and protein substructures [Evangelista21].

In addition to cAMP, it has been demonstrated that other nucleotides (ppGpp, GTP, cGMP, and ATP) bind to CRP with a similar affinity as cAMP, suggesting a modulatory effect of these nucleotides on the protein [Duysak21].

It has been observed that when cAMP is absent, mutations in CRP allow it to compensate for the absence of cAMP; also, it has been shown that CRP with the A144T dominant mutation is activated in the presence of cytidine or uridine. In addition, cytidine and uracil appear to inhibit the activity of wild-type CRP, suggesting that these nucleosides bind to the transcription factor [Lauritsen21].

Mechanism of transcriptional regulation

CRP binds to a 22-bp symmetrical site [Ebright89] and induces a severe bend upon binding, with an angle of ~80° [Schultz91a, Parkinson96, Wu, Chen01p]. Interdependence was observed for neighboring DNA bases in the 22-bp site, for example, between positions 1 and 2, 6 and 8, and 16 and 19 [Vahed19].

Two regions of CRP, AR1 (\"activation region 1\"), located in the C-terminal domain [Zhou93c, Niu94], and AR2 [Niu96], located in the N-terminal domain, are known to interact with RNA polymerase (RNAP).

Promoters that are activated by cAMP-CRP can be grouped into three classes, termed class I, class II, and class III promoters [Busby99a]. Class I- and class II-dependent promoters require one cAMP-CRP for activation and have a single DNA-binding site located upstream of the RNAP-binding site, centered near position -93, -83, -72, or -62 of class I promoters [Ushida90, Gaston90, Tebbutt02] and overlapping the RNAP-binding site of class II promoters [Busby99a]. At class I promoters, AR1 of the downstream subunit of the CRP dimer interacts with the α-CTD of RNAP [Zhou94a], thereby increasing the affinity of RNAP for the promoter DNA [Igarashi91, Savery96, Ebright93].

Class II-dependent promoters require AR1 of the upstream subunit and AR2 of the downstream subunit of CRP. AR1 recruits α-CTD to the DNA region upstream of the bound CRP dimer, while AR2 interacts with α-NTD of RNAP [Savery96, Niu96, Savery98]. It was suggested that CRP at class II-dependent promoters induces a conformational change in the RNAP causing an open cleft that facilitates entry of the DNA promoter [Shi20]. Class III promoters require multiple activator molecules, that is, either two or more CAP dimers or one CRP dimer and additional activator proteins synergistically activate transcription [Barnard04, Beatty03]. Dependent on the localization of its binding site, CRP functions by a class I or class II mechanism at class III promoters or by a more complex mechanism which can involve direct interactions with the second activator [Belyaeva00, Wade01, Wickstrum05], or CRP exerts its function by DNA bending [Savery96, Busby99a, Lobell91].

CRP represses transcription by promoter occlusion [Kolb93], by exclusion of an activator protein [Polayes88], through the interaction with a repressor protein in an antiactivation mechanism [Mollegaard93, ValentinHansen96, McNeill07, Perini96] or by hindering promoter clearance [Liu04k, Rostoks00].

cAMP-CRP is a positive regulator necessary for the induction of the viable but nonculturable (VBNC) state in response to cold and starvation conditions [Nosho18a]. rpoS has a minor role in the effect of cAMP-CRP, but there is a cAMP-CRP-specific pathway independent of rpoS expression that contributes to regulation of the formation of VBNC and regulates the formation of VBNC cells more markedly than RpoS itself [Nosho18a]. CRP is a major contributor for H2S generation coupled to thiosulfate assimilation during glucose starvation, perhaps through the control of unknown genes; the mechanism(s) for this action during glucose starvation is not yet known [Tanaka19a].

ZnO quantum dots (QDs) are nanoparticles known for their antimicrobial activity; they bind to CRP and inhibit its transcription activity [Saha18].

Based on two sets of previously published data (on the genome-wide scale) crossed with the different conditions of glucose availability, and using an optimized microarray method (Q-GDEMAR), the regulatory acetylation mechanisms [deacetylase CobB, peptidyl N()-lysine acetyltransferase PatZ] exerted by the DNA-binding dual regulator CRP-cAMP and their relation with glucose availability were analyzed [Guebel18]. CRP not only is an effector of catabolite repression, but also it acts under all the glucose conditions tested (excess, limited, and exhausted), exerting both positive and negative effects through different sets of genes [Guebel18]. The extensive changes produced in specific subsets of genes both CRP-deacetylated and CRP-acetylated are glucose dependent [Guebel18].

By measuring and modeling allelic manifolds, the in vivo Gibbs free energy (DG) of CRP-RNAP interactions that occur at a variety of different binding site spacings were determined and measured to an estimated precision of ~ 0.1 kcal/mol. DG values for in vivo CRP-DNA and σ70RNAP-DNA interactions were also obtained, with similar estimated precision [Forcier18]. This model can be used to dissect cis-regulatory biophysics in living cells [Forcier18].

Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of CRP appears to increase [Deter21].

Catabolite repression and inducer exclusion

Catabolite repression in E. coli is mediated by the interplay of CRP, adenylate cyclase, cAMP, and the glucose-specific enzyme IIA (EIIAGlc) of the phosphoenolpyruvate:sugar phosphotransferase system [Deutscher08, Deutscher06, Gorke08]. Catabolite repression by cAMP/CRP regulates the total carbon uptake flux through a negative feedback loop [Hermsen15]. In the absence of rapidly metabolizable carbon sources, such as glucose, EIIAGlc is phosphorylated [Hogema98] and activates adenylate cyclase [Feucht80, Reddy98a], resulting in an elevated level of cAMP [Park06a, Bettenbrock07]. Due to the autoregulation of crp [Aiba83, Ishizuka94, Hanamura92], cAMP-CRP levels increase. In addition, in the presence of unphosphorylated EIIAGlc, inducer is transported into the cell, leading to the inactivation of the corresponding repressor molecules [Saier89, Magasanik70]. Therefore, transcription of catabolic genes is switched on by cAMP-CRP.

If glucose is available, EIIAGlc is predominantly dephosphorylated [Hogema98]. As a consequence, adenylate cyclase is not activated, resulting in a reduced level of cAMP. Due to the autoregulation of crp, cAMP-CRP levels decrease [Hanamura91]. In addition, EIIAGlc blocks the uptake of inducer by blocking the transport systems (\"inducer exclusion\") [Nelson83, Osumi82, Dills82, Sondej02]. Thus, transcription of catabolic genes is switched off. cAMP not only mediates carbon metabolism but also plays a physiological role to ensure that proteomic resources are spent on distinct metabolic pathways as needed in different nutrient environments [You13]. α-Keto-acids inhibit cAMP production [You13]. cAMP-CRP reduce cell width under nutrient-poor conditions through their impact on the morphogenic factor BolA, and they reduce cell length through action on FtsZ assembly [Westfall18].

Based on wild-type and recombinant cells cultivated in two different substrates (lactose and glycerol), the effect of phosphate-starved response (PSR) stimuli was investigated. Gene expression analysis showed that under PSR conditions, selected genes (gapA, pykF, ppsA, icdA) in the glycolysis and pentose phosphate pathways (zwf, gnd, talB, tktA) were up-regulated, whereas other genes in lactose (lacY, lacA) and acetate (ackA, pta) metabolism pathways were down-regulated. It was also demonstrated that Cra, CRP transcription factors, and the PhoBR two-component signal transduction system are involved in the regulation of central carbon metabolism [Pandi20].

CRP has been adapted to respond to different external and internal stimuli according to the particular ecological niches occupied by the bacterium [Green14]. CRP is a key regulator in metabolism of cell persisters [Mok15]. CRP has an important role during growth at low temperatures [Uppal15].

A cAMP-CRP-controlled mechanism for the incorporation of extracellular ADP-glucose involves NupC and NupG nucleoside transporters [Almagro18]. cAMP maintains the correct cellular aspect ratio [Westfall18].

Gene Expression

crp gene expression is upregulated upon L-valine addition (isoleucine starvation) in the cellular growth medium; this effect was observed during the first 5 minutes of the amino acid addition, but then crp expression dropped [Gummesson20].

In the complementary strand of the 5Â´region of the gene crp is encoded an antisense RNA, sensitive to RNAse III, that could regulate the expression of crp [Lejars22].

Mutants

CRP was engineered to prove the enhanced strain osmotolerance phenotype based on several random mutagenesis studies. All variants showed much higher osmotolerance towards NaCl and others osmotic stressors, such as KCl, glucose, and sucrose, than the wild type [Zhang12w]. Using DNA microarray analysis, genes involved in colanic acid biosynthesis were identified as upregulated in the absence of salt stress, whereas carbohydrate metabolism genes were differentially expressed under NaCl stress in MT6 (a CRP mutant with the highest osmotolerance towards NaCl) compared to the wild type [Zhang12w].

The Gly184 residue of CRP is important to its function as a transcriptional activator, and alteration of this residue affects its DNA binding and probably its RNA polymerase interaction [Hicks17].

The growth and the net final biomass produced in a crp single deletion mutant strain growing under anaerobic fermentation conditions were affected relative to responses of the wild-type strain (Escherichia coli strain BW 25113) grown in the same conditions [Kargeti17].

A library of synthetic complex promoters was developed for the global regulators CRP and IHF; the promoters were formed by a weak 35/10 consensus sequence preceded by four combinatorial binding sites for these two TFs [Monteiro18]. CRP and IHF have very different regulatory effects: cis elements for CRP preferentially activate promoters when located immediately upstream of the promoter consensus, while binding sites for IHF mainly function as UP elements and transcription is stimulated in several different architectures in the absence of this protein [Monteiro18]. The extrapolation of these properties of complex synthetic promoters to naturally occurring regulatory systems could significantly impact the engineering of synthetic biological circuits in bacteria [Monteiro18].

Deletion of global transcription regulators such as Fnr, ArcA, IHF, CRP, and Fis under anaerobic fermentation conditions increased the glucose uptake rate above that required for the observed growth rate. In addition, higher ATP synthesis and redox balance rates were reported relative to the observed growth rate and biomass yield [Kargeti18].

A crp knockout appears to decrease sodium deoxycholate (DOC) susceptibility in the absence of the multidrug efflux pump AcrAB-TolC [Le20]. The same knockout decreases cell growth, lowers cell density in the stationary phase, and forms a smaller colony than the parent strain [Le20].

A CRP knockout mutant showed disruption of proteome allocation and metabolic alterations under glucose respiratory conditions during mid-exponential phase, which lead to a reduction in growth rate of approximately 57% and correlated with reduced glucose and oxygen uptake rates and high accumulation of cAMP, while the biomass yield was not perturbed [Pal22]. Differential transcription analysis of CRP in the knockout strain compared to the wild-type strain showed ~74% of differentially expressed genes were downregulated; these downregulated genes were mostly σ70 dependent, while the other 26% were upregulated and mainly dependent on other stress-related σ factors [Pal22]. In the CRP knockout, mutant genes involved in the TCA cycle, uronic acid, galactitol, glucan, glucose, amino acids, nucleotides, and alternative sources of carbon metabolism were downregulated [Pal22].

Based on adaptative laboratory evolution of the CRP knockout mutant, five independent strains with seemingly preperturbed growth and proteome allocation were obtained, but these mutant strains showed a reduced biomass yield; the most relevant mutations for phenotype recovery were in the ptsG promoter, which could potentially enhance the affinity of RNA polymerase σ70 for this promoter [Pal22]. Evolved CRP knockout strains showed increased ptsG gene expression and glucose uptake, while stress-related genes upregulated in the parental CRP knockout strain were expressed in a pattern similar to the wild-type strain [Pal22].

In E. coli the presence of exogenous glucose or crp gene disruption confer protection to attacks by some T6SS effectors from V. cholerae [Crisan21], indicating that CRP likely directly or indirectly represses one or various genes that confer protection against some T6SS attacks which are active in the presence of glucose [Crisan21].

E. coli is able to acquire high hydrostatic pressure resistance when the activities of CRP, Cra, and the glyoxylate shunt are decreased and the activities of RpoH and RpoS are increased [Gayan20].

The importance of indirect readout for the nucleosome as well as of the bacterial regulators Fis and CRP was determined by using the software ThreaDNA. ThreaDNA can be used to predict the contribution of DNA deformations for the sequence selectivity of proteins [Cevost18].

In review articles about CRP, the role that CRP orthologs play in different bacterial species [SoberonChavez17] and results of studies with CRP mutants were reviewed [Frendorf19].

A missense mutation in the crp gene compensates for a knockout mutation in the genes encoding the major antibiotic efflux pumps AcrAB and AcrEF through derepression of genes enconding the MdtEF efflux pump [Cho21a].

Cellular exposure to quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs), which are used as antimicrobial agents, causes mutation in the crp gene [Jia22].

A crp knockout mutant made E. coli an insect mutualist [Koga22].

<p>
It has been observed that when cAMP is absent, mutations in CRP allow it to compensate for the absence of cAMP; also, it has been shown that CRP with the A144T dominant mutation is activated in the presence of cytidine or uridine. In addition, cytidine and uracil appear to inhibit the activity of wild-type CRP, suggesting that these nucleosides bind to the transcription factor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34620864">Lauritsen21</a>].  
<p>
<b>Mechanism of transcriptional regulation</b>
<p>
CRP binds to a 22-bp symmetrical site [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2557589">Ebright89</a>] and induces a severe bend upon binding, with an angle of ~80&deg; [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1653449">Schultz91a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8757802">Parkinson96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6323997">Wu</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11724533">Chen01p</a>].  Interdependence was observed  for neighboring DNA bases in the 22-bp site, for example, between positions 1 and  2, 6 and 8, and 16 and 19 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31469855">Vahed19</a>].
<p>
Two regions of CRP, AR1 (\"activation region 1\"), located in the C-terminal domain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8392187">Zhou93c</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7966284">Niu94</a>], and AR2 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8978616">Niu96</a>], located in the N-terminal domain, are known to interact with RNA polymerase (RNAP). 
<p>
Promoters that are activated by cAMP-CRP can be grouped into three classes, termed class I, class II, and class III promoters [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10550204">Busby99a</a>]. Class I- and class II-dependent promoters require one cAMP-CRP for activation and have a single DNA-binding site located upstream of the RNAP-binding site, centered near position -93, -83, -72, or -62 of class I promoters [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2173826">Ushida90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2167178">Gaston90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12023077">Tebbutt02</a>] and overlapping the RNAP-binding site of class II promoters [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10550204">Busby99a</a>]. At class I promoters, AR1 of the downstream subunit of the CRP dimer interacts with the &alpha;-CTD of RNAP [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7925296">Zhou94a</a>], thereby increasing the affinity of RNAP for the promoter DNA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1646077">Igarashi91</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8735277">Savery96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8394979">Ebright93</a>].
<p>
Class II-dependent promoters require AR1 of the upstream subunit and AR2 of the downstream subunit of CRP. AR1 recruits &alpha;-CTD to the DNA region upstream of the bound CRP dimer, while AR2 interacts with &alpha;-NTD of RNAP [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8735277">Savery96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8978616">Niu96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9628879">Savery98</a>]. It was suggested that CRP at class II-dependent promoters induces a conformational change in the RNAP causing an open cleft that facilitates entry of the DNA promoter [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32310937">Shi20</a>]. Class III promoters require multiple activator molecules, that is, either two or more CAP dimers or one CRP dimer and additional activator proteins synergistically activate transcription [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15063844">Barnard04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12923087">Beatty03</a>]. Dependent on the localization of its binding site, CRP functions by a class I or class II mechanism at class III promoters or by a more complex mechanism which can involve direct interactions with the second activator [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10760178">Belyaeva00</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11742992">Wade01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16166533">Wickstrum05</a>], or CRP exerts its function by DNA bending [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8735277">Savery96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10550204">Busby99a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1848302">Lobell91</a>].
<p>
CRP represses transcription by promoter occlusion [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8394684">Kolb93</a>], by exclusion of an activator protein [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2454912">Polayes88</a>], through the interaction with a repressor protein in an antiactivation mechanism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8394345">Mollegaard93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8736525">ValentinHansen96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17158559">McNeill07</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8969182">Perini96</a>] or by hindering promoter clearance [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15385551">Liu04k</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10760580">Rostoks00</a>].  
<p>
cAMP-CRP is a positive regulator necessary for the induction of the viable but nonculturable (VBNC) state in response to cold and starvation conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29458560">Nosho18a</a>]. <i>rpoS</i> has a minor role in the effect of cAMP-CRP, but there is a cAMP-CRP-specific pathway independent of <i>rpoS</i> expression that contributes to regulation of the formation of VBNC and regulates the formation of VBNC cells more markedly than RpoS itself [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29458560">Nosho18a</a>]. CRP is a major contributor for H<sub>2</sub>S generation coupled to thiosulfate assimilation during glucose starvation, perhaps through the control of unknown genes; the mechanism(s) for this action during glucose starvation is not yet known [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30880290">Tanaka19a</a>].
<p>
ZnO quantum dots (QDs) are nanoparticles known for their antimicrobial activity; they bind to CRP and inhibit its transcription activity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29870809">Saha18</a>].
<p>
Based on two sets of previously published data (on the genome-wide scale) crossed with the different conditions of glucose availability, and using an optimized microarray method (Q-GDEMAR), the regulatory acetylation mechanisms [deacetylase CobB, peptidyl N()-lysine acetyltransferase PatZ] exerted by the DNA-binding dual regulator CRP-cAMP and their relation with glucose availability were analyzed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29875739">Guebel18</a>]. CRP not only is an effector of catabolite repression, but also it acts under all the glucose conditions tested (excess, limited, and exhausted), exerting both positive and negative effects through different sets of genes [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29875739">Guebel18</a>]. The extensive changes produced in specific subsets of genes both CRP-deacetylated and CRP-acetylated are glucose dependent [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29875739">Guebel18</a>].
<p>
By measuring and modeling allelic manifolds, the <i>in vivo</i> Gibbs free energy (DG) of CRP-RNAP interactions that occur at a variety of different binding site spacings were determined and measured to an estimated precision of ~ 0.1 kcal/mol. DG values for <i>in vivo</i> CRP-DNA and &sigma;<sup>70</sup>RNAP-DNA interactions were also obtained, with similar estimated precision [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30570483">Forcier18</a>]. This model can be used to dissect cis-regulatory biophysics in living cells [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30570483">Forcier18</a>].
<p>
Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of CRP appears to increase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33731833">Deter21</a>].
<p>
<b>Catabolite repression and inducer exclusion</b>
<p>
Catabolite repression in <i>E. coli</i> is mediated by the interplay of CRP, adenylate cyclase, cAMP, and the glucose-specific enzyme IIA (EIIA<sup>Glc</sup>) of the phosphoenolpyruvate:sugar phosphotransferase system [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18359269">Deutscher08</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17158705">Deutscher06</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18628769">Gorke08</a>]. Catabolite repression by cAMP/CRP regulates the total carbon uptake flux through a negative feedback loop [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25862745">Hermsen15</a>]. In the absence of rapidly metabolizable carbon sources, such as glucose, EIIA<sup>Glc</sup> is phosphorylated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9822815">Hogema98</a>] and activates adenylate cyclase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6245052">Feucht80</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9457881">Reddy98a</a>], resulting in an elevated level of cAMP [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16407219">Park06a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17675376">Bettenbrock07</a>]. Due to the autoregulation of <i>crp</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6297782">Aiba83</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7518773">Ishizuka94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1328816">Hanamura92</a>], cAMP-CRP levels increase. In addition, in the presence of unphosphorylated EIIA<sup>Glc</sup>, inducer is transported into the cell, leading to the inactivation of the corresponding repressor molecules [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2651862">Saier89</a>, <a href="/ECOLI/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bMagasanik70%5d">Magasanik70</a>]. Therefore, transcription of catabolic genes is switched on by cAMP-CRP.
<p>
If glucose is available, EIIA<sup>Glc</sup> is predominantly dephosphorylated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9822815">Hogema98</a>]. As a consequence, adenylate cyclase is not activated, resulting in a reduced level of cAMP. Due to the autoregulation of <i>crp</i>, cAMP-CRP levels decrease [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1715982">Hanamura91</a>]. In addition, EIIA<sup>Glc</sup> blocks the uptake of inducer by blocking the transport systems (\"inducer exclusion\") [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16453452">Nelson83</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7041121">Osumi82</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7040431">Dills82</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11969416">Sondej02</a>]. Thus, transcription of catabolic genes is switched off. cAMP not only mediates carbon metabolism but also plays a physiological role to ensure that proteomic resources are spent on distinct metabolic pathways as needed in different nutrient environments [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23925119">You13</a>]. &alpha;-Keto-acids inhibit cAMP production [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23925119">You13</a>]. cAMP-CRP reduce cell width under nutrient-poor conditions through their impact on the morphogenic factor BolA, and they reduce cell length through action on FtsZ assembly [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29432413">Westfall18</a>].
<p>
Based on wild-type and recombinant cells cultivated in two different substrates (lactose and glycerol), the effect of phosphate-starved response (PSR) stimuli was investigated. Gene expression analysis showed that under PSR conditions, selected genes (<i>gapA, pykF, ppsA, icdA</i>) in the glycolysis and pentose phosphate pathways (<i>zwf, gnd, talB, tktA</i>) were up-regulated, whereas other genes in lactose (<i>lacY, lacA</i>) and acetate (<i>ackA, pta</i>) metabolism pathways were down-regulated. It was also demonstrated that Cra, CRP transcription factors, and the PhoBR two-component signal transduction system are involved in the regulation of central carbon metabolism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33001250">Pandi20</a>]. 
<p>
CRP has been adapted to respond to different external and internal stimuli according to the particular ecological niches occupied by the bacterium [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24509484">Green14</a>]. CRP is a key regulator in metabolism of cell persisters [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25712354">Mok15</a>]. CRP has an important role during growth at low temperatures [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25637299">Uppal15</a>].
<p>
A cAMP-CRP-controlled mechanism for the incorporation of extracellular ADP-glucose involves NupC and NupG nucleoside transporters [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30341391">Almagro18</a>]. cAMP maintains the correct cellular aspect ratio [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29432413">Westfall18</a>].
<p>
<b>Gene Expression</b>
<p>
<i>crp</i> gene expression is upregulated upon L-valine addition (isoleucine starvation) in the cellular growth medium; this effect was observed during the first 5 minutes of the amino acid addition, but then <i>crp</i> expression dropped [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32211022">Gummesson20</a>].
<p>
In the complementary strand of the 5Â´region of the gene <i>crp</i> is encoded an antisense RNA, sensitive to RNAse III, that could regulate the expression of <i>crp</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/36000733">Lejars22</a>]. 
<p>
<b>Mutants</b>
<p>
CRP was engineered to prove the enhanced strain osmotolerance phenotype based on several random mutagenesis studies. All variants showed much higher osmotolerance towards NaCl and others osmotic stressors, such as KCl, glucose, and sucrose, than the wild type [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22179860">Zhang12w</a>]. Using DNA microarray analysis, genes involved in colanic acid biosynthesis were identified as upregulated in the absence of salt stress, whereas carbohydrate metabolism genes were differentially expressed under NaCl stress in MT6 (a CRP mutant with the highest osmotolerance towards NaCl) compared to the wild type [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22179860">Zhang12w</a>].
<p>
The Gly184 residue of CRP is important to its function as a transcriptional activator, and alteration of this residue affects its DNA binding and probably its RNA polymerase interaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28956357">Hicks17</a>].
<p>
The growth and the net final biomass produced in a <i>crp</i> single deletion mutant strain growing under anaerobic fermentation conditions were affected relative to responses of the wild-type strain (<i>Escherichia coli</i> strain BW 25113) grown in the same conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28573283">Kargeti17</a>].
<p>
A library of synthetic complex promoters was developed for the global regulators CRP and IHF; the promoters were formed by a weak 35/10 consensus sequence preceded by four combinatorial binding sites for these two TFs [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29091423">Monteiro18</a>]. CRP and IHF have very different regulatory effects: <i>cis</i> elements for CRP preferentially activate promoters when located immediately upstream of the promoter consensus, while binding sites for IHF mainly function as UP elements and transcription is stimulated in several different architectures in the absence of this protein [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29091423">Monteiro18</a>]. The extrapolation of these properties of complex synthetic promoters to naturally occurring regulatory systems could significantly impact the engineering of synthetic biological circuits in bacteria [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29091423">Monteiro18</a>].
<p>
Deletion of global transcription regulators such as Fnr, ArcA, IHF, CRP, and Fis under anaerobic fermentation conditions increased the glucose uptake rate above that required for the observed growth rate. In addition, higher ATP synthesis and redox balance rates were reported relative to the observed growth rate and biomass yield [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29748694">Kargeti18</a>].
<p>
A <i>crp</i> knockout appears to decrease sodium deoxycholate (DOC) susceptibility in the absence of the multidrug efflux pump AcrAB-TolC [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32407499">Le20</a>].  The same knockout decreases cell growth, lowers cell density in the stationary phase, and forms a smaller colony than the parent strain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32407499">Le20</a>].  
<p>
A CRP knockout mutant showed disruption of proteome allocation and metabolic alterations under glucose respiratory conditions during mid-exponential phase, which lead to a reduction in growth rate of approximately 57% and correlated with reduced glucose and oxygen uptake rates and high accumulation of cAMP, while the biomass yield was not perturbed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35167766">Pal22</a>]. Differential transcription analysis of CRP in the knockout strain compared to the wild-type strain showed ~74% of differentially expressed genes were downregulated; these downregulated genes were mostly &sigma;<sup>70</sup> dependent, while the other 26% were upregulated and mainly dependent on other stress-related &sigma; factors [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35167766">Pal22</a>]. In the CRP knockout, mutant genes involved in the TCA cycle, uronic acid, galactitol, glucan, glucose, amino acids, nucleotides, and alternative sources of carbon metabolism were downregulated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35167766">Pal22</a>].
<p>
Based on adaptative laboratory evolution of the CRP knockout mutant, five independent strains with seemingly preperturbed growth and proteome allocation were obtained, but these mutant strains showed a reduced biomass yield; the most relevant mutations for phenotype recovery were in the <i>ptsG</i> promoter, which could potentially enhance the affinity of RNA polymerase &sigma;<sup>70</sup> for this promoter [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35167766">Pal22</a>]. Evolved CRP knockout strains showed increased <i>ptsG</i> gene expression and glucose uptake, while stress-related genes upregulated in the parental CRP knockout strain were expressed in a pattern similar to the wild-type strain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35167766">Pal22</a>].
<p>
In <i>E. coli</i> the presence of exogenous glucose or crp gene disruption confer protection to attacks by some T6SS effectors from <i>V. cholerae</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33536444">Crisan21</a>], indicating that CRP likely directly or indirectly represses one or various genes that confer protection against some T6SS attacks which are active in the presence of glucose [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33536444">Crisan21</a>].
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> is able to acquire high hydrostatic pressure resistance when the activities of CRP, Cra, and the glyoxylate shunt are decreased and the activities of RpoH and RpoS are increased [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32979485">Gayan20</a>].
<p>
The importance of indirect readout for the nucleosome as well as of the bacterial regulators Fis and CRP was determined by using the software ThreaDNA. ThreaDNA can be used to predict the contribution of DNA deformations for the sequence selectivity of proteins [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29444234">Cevost18</a>].
<p>
In review articles about CRP, the role that CRP orthologs play in different bacterial species [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28620358">SoberonChavez17</a>] and results of studies with CRP mutants were reviewed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31303977">Frendorf19</a>].
<p>
A missense mutation in the <i>crp</i> gene compensates for a knockout mutation in the genes encoding the major antibiotic efflux pumps AcrAB and AcrEF through derepression of genes enconding the MdtEF efflux pump [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33972351">Cho21a</a>].
<p>
Cellular exposure to quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs), which are used as antimicrobial agents, causes mutation in the <i>crp</i> gene [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35398118">Jia22</a>].
<p>
A <i>crp</i> knockout mutant made <i>E. coli</i> an insect mutualist [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35927448">Koga22</a>].</comment>

slots.text:
Lrp, "Leucine-responsive regulatory protein," is a dual transcriptional regulator for at least 10% of the genes in Escherichia coli [Tani02]. These genes are involved in amino acid biosynthesis and catabolism, nutrient transport, pili synthesis, and other cellular functions, including 1-carbon metabolism [Ernsting92, Brinkman03, Calvo94]. In addition, Lrp affects nearly three-fourths of the genes induced upon entry into stationary phase [Tani02, Cho08]. Lrp might also play a topological role in dynamic DNA packaging [DAri93]. Using a machine learning framework that integrates and analyzes data from 10 different sources, it was determined that Lrp is involved in antibiotic resistance in E. coli, and this was confirmed in Salmonella enterica [Youn22].

Lrp can act as a repressor or activator for its target genes. Binding of leucine can affect these activities in three different ways: leucine either potentiates, antagonizes, or has no discernible effect upon Lrp action [Lin92c, Platko93, Newman95a]. It is believed that Lrp senses the presence of rich nutrition based on the concentration of leucine and positively regulates genes that function during famine and negatively regulates genes that function during a feast [Calvo94].

Lrp forms a mixture of octamers and hexadecamers [Chen01m]. In the presence of leucine, the octamer configuration is favored. It is believed that the switch between the octameric and hexadecameric states modulated by leucine affects the binding and the activity of Lrp at its target genes [Chen02m]. The structure of Lrp from Escherichia coli bound to DNA as an octamer has been solved [delosRios07]. Lrp forms an open ring structure, in which the DNA is wrapped around the octamer in a nucleosome-like structure. The monomer chain contains two domains, an N-terminal helix-turn-helix motif and a C-terminal αβ-sandwich fold.

The N-terminal is responsible for the specificity and function among members of the Lrp regulon across the Enterobacteriaceae. The N-terminal tail plays a significant role in modulating Lrp function, similar to what has been reported for a number of other transcriptional regulators [Hart11].

N-terminal diversity is responsible for some of the differences between Lrp TF orthologs in terms of DNA binding and multimerization [Hart11].

Lrp-regulated promoters commonly contain multiple adjacent binding sites for the protein with low sequence specificity. A consensus recognition sequence has been described [Cui96]. The identified 15-bp sequence motif is structured with flanking CAG/CTG triplets and a central AT-rich signal. Leucine has two effects upon binding to DNA in vitro: the affinity of Lrp is reduced but the cooperativity of binding to multiple sites is increased [Chen05k].

It has been observed that in E. coli the major stability and affinity of Lrp to DNA is at neutral pH conditions, although the cooperativity increases as the pH declines [Ishii21]. However, it appears that Lrp can be adapted to other conditions in other bacteria, such as Lrp of Komagataeibacter europaeus, which is more stable and functional under acidic pH [Ishii21].

Lrp belongs to the Lrp/AsnC family of transcriptional regulatory proteins, which is widely distributed throughout the eubacterial and archaeal domains. Lrp appears to be very well conserved in members of the γ-proteobacteria [Brinkman03]. Based on phylogenetic and Logo analysis, a conserved signature in the Lrp TF and its paralog, AscN, were identified in γ-proteobacteria [Unoarumhi16]. Likewise, specific residues that correlated with global versus local regulatory roles were determined [Unoarumhi16].

A microarray analysis for Lrp of Escherichia coli was done by [Hung02a].

Based on whole-proteome analysis, three lysines (K28, K39, and K132) were identified as points of acetylation [Baeza14].

Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of Lrp appears to increase [Deter21].

Using Bayesian hierarchical models, genes in the amino acid metabolism sRNA pathway were identified as coexpressed with serA gene changes according to the level of Lrp under various biological conditions [Kinzy19].

Likewise, specific residues that correlated with global versus local regulatory roles were determined [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27206730">Unoarumhi16</a>].
<p>
A microarray analysis for Lrp of <i>Escherichia coli</i> was done by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12130640">Hung02a</a>].
<p>
Based on whole-proteome analysis, three lysines (K28, K39, and K132) were identified as points of acetylation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24917678">Baeza14</a>].
<p>
Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of Lrp appears to increase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33731833">Deter21</a>].
<p>
Using Bayesian hierarchical models, genes in the amino acid metabolism sRNA pathway were identified as coexpressed with <i>serA</i> gene changes according to the level of Lrp under various biological conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30735484">Kinzy19</a>].</comment>
