slots.text:
ArcA is a dual transcriptional regulator for Anoxic redox control [Iuchi88, Iuchi93, Gunsalus94]. It acts primarily as a negative transcriptional regulator under anaerobic conditions. ArcA represses operons involved in respiratory metabolism, including those that encode products such as the tricarboxylic acid cycle enzymes, enzymes of the glyoxylate shunt, and enzymes of the pathway for fatty acid degradation [Iuchi91, Gunsalus94, Lin91]. In addition, ArcA acts as a repressor for rpoS transcription [Mika05]. ArcA also activates a few operons encoding proteins involved in fermentative metabolism [Brondsted94, Lynch96]. It has been identified as global repressor of carbon oxidation pathways [Park13d]. Microarray analyses have identified a large number of genes affected by ArcA and have revealed that the Arc system and the FNR regulatory network overlap to a much greater extent than previously estimated [Salmon05, Liu04a, Perrenoud05, Iyer21]. It has been suggested that the most significant role of ArcA is under microaerobic conditions, while that of FNR is under more strictly anaerobic conditions [Alexeeva03, Levanon05]. For full expression of arcA both FNR and ArcA are required [Compan94]. Distinct functional roles for both regulators have been proposed, and it has been shown that there is little direct coregulation of the two [Park13d].

ArcA is a response regulator and is activated as a DNA-binding protein by phosphorylation [Jeon01]. The cognate sensor kinase ArcB is membrane associated and has three cytoplasmic domains; a transmitter, a receiver, and a phosphotransfer (HPt) domain [Ishige94, Iuchi92a]. Under anaerobic conditions ArcA is phosphorylated in a phosphorelay reaction that involves phosphotransfer from the autophosphorylated transmitter domain of ArcB to the receiver and Hpt domain of ArcB and finally to the receiver domain of ArcA [Kwon00c, Tsuzuki95, Georgellis97]. Autophosphorylation of ArcB is stimulated by effectors such as d-lactate, pyruvate, and acetate [Georgellis99, Georgellis99]. Under aerobic conditions, the autokinase activity of ArcB is inhibited by quinone electron carriers [Georgellis01, Malpica04], and unphosphorylated ArcB promotes the dephosphorylation of ArcA-P by a reverse phosphorelay reaction [Georgellis98, PenaSandoval05]. It has been suggested that ArcA may also be subject to cross-regulation by other, unknown sensor kinases [Mika05, Oshima02, Kato07a]. Z nucleotides [ZMP (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide-1-beta-D-ribofuranosyl 5-monophosphate) and/or ZTP (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide-1-beta-D-ribofuranosyl 5-triphosphate)] can act as direct phosphodonors to ArcA in vivo, activating it in an ArcB-independent manner [VazquezCiros20].

ArcA is a member of the OmpR/PhoB subfamily of response regulators and consists of an N-terminal receiver domain and a C-terminal helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain [Mizuno97]. The crystal structures of the receiver domain of ArcA in the presence and absence of the phosphoryl analog BeF3- have been solved [ToroRoman05a]. In the crystal structures, the receiver domain forms a symmetric dimer.

ArcA appears to be S-nitrosylated on Cys173 in planktonic cells under aerobic growth conditions [Barraud21].

Weight matrices for the DNA-binding site for ArcA-P have been obtained. The proposed binding site consists of 15 bp with a direct spaced repeat [Favorov05, McGuire99]. It has been suggested that multimerization, induced by phosphorylation, is a prerequisite for binding [Jeon01]. ArcA represses transcription by directly binding to the promoter or by binding to sites overlapping an activator-binding site [Cho06a, Jeong04b]. As an activator, it appears to act as part of a nucleoprotein complex. For activation of pfl, a functional interaction between the ArcA and Fnr protein has been suggested [Sawers92]. For expression of cydAB, it has been shown that ArcA-P antagonizes H-NS [Govantes00]. At the R1 PY promoter, ArcA acts in conjunction with TraJ. ArcA represses and activates transcription solely by binding DNA, and it activates only indirectly when its binding interferes with the binding and repression of another transcriptional repressor [Park13d]. The majority of ArcA-binding sites overlap the σ70 promoter recognition elements [Park13d].

ArcA is not an essential protein [Miyake20]. Under glucose-abundant conditions, the double mutant of iclR arcA causes an increase in biomass yield (47%) and reduction of acetate (70%) and CO2 (16%) production. Under glucose-limited conditions, this double mutant exhibits an increase of biomass of only 13% [Waegeman11]. On the other hand, in an arcA mutant, the TCA cycle flux was increased 4.4 times above that of the wild type in the presence of nitrates, and the intracellular ATP/ADP ratio increased approximately 2-fold above that of the wild-type strain [Toya12].

An exhaustive analysis of the ArcA response regulator was carried out, based on different experimental methodologies, High-throughputs (ChIP-chip and ChIP-seq), bioinformatic analysis, DNase I footprinting, and gene expression profiling, and the results showed that ArcA is a global repressor of carbon oxidation pathways [Park13d]. ArcA-P directly regulates the expression of 85 operons under anaerobic growth conditions, where 74 operons are repressed and 11 are activated [Park13d]. The proportion of phosphorylated ArcA is increased in aerobic conditions and the presence of carbon monoxide (CO) [Wareham16]. It was shown that most ArcA-binding sites contain additional direct repeat (DR) elements as well as the two required for binding an ArcA dimer, and this finding provided a novel insight into how ArcA accomplishes global regulation of gene expression [Park13d]. More than 50% of the sites have additional DR elements, and the majority of ArcA-binding sites contain three to five DR elements, predominantly at a CTC spacing of 11 bp [Park13d]. The variations in the number, spacing, location, and predicted strength of DR elements within the chromosomal ArcA-binding regions suggest plasticity in the architecture of ArcA-binding sites for either repressed or activated operons [Park13d].

The growth [Iyer21, Kargeti17] and the net final biomass produced in an arcA single-deletion mutants growing under anaerobic fermentation conditions were affected relative to responses of the wild-type strain (Escherichia coli strain BW25113) grown in the same conditions [Kargeti17]. arcA deletion increased expression of genes involved in acetate assimilation and uptake and also genes involved in the TCA cycle [Veeravalli18, Iyer21]. The mutant also caused decreased nucleotide synthesis, decreased glucose and ammonia uptake rates, and enhanced nitrogen transport and accumulation of amino acids and their precursors, as well as derepression of alternate carbon metabolic proteins [Iyer21]. The activities of some transcription factors appear to be enhanced (ArgR, NtrC, NrdR) in the arcA mutant, whereas others are diminished (PuuR) [Iyer21]. [Kargeti18] et al. reported a relative increase in glucose uptake rate above that required for the observed growth rate in an arcA mutant. In addition, higher ATP synthesis and redox balance rates were reported relative to the observed growth rate and biomass yield in the mutant [Kargeti18].

ArcA promotes dehydration tolerance, both independently and through ArcZ or RpoS [Chen18c].

The accumulation of the protein ArcA is decreased during iron-limiting conditions [Zupok19]. A negative correlation between cellular growth and the copy number of the proteins ArcA has been reported [Parisutham22].

ArcA is a flux sensor for the oxygen consumption rate [Nochino20].

Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of ArcA appears to increase [Deter21].

Deletion of arcA and gutM under three different antibiotics, cefixime, ciprofloxacin, and chloramphenicol, significantly suppressed resistance evolution, which was not caused by epistatic interactions with mutations known to confer drug resistance [Horinouchi20].

When cells are grown in acetate as a carbon source, the knockout mutants of arcA and fis show an improved growth rate and enhanced acetate uptake [Jindal22]. This is a consequence of the reprogramming of the carbon metabolic flux generated by the mutants [Jindal22].

A review of the regulation of molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis and molybdoenzyme gene expression via molybdenum and iron by FNR, NarXL/QP, Fur, and ArcA has been published [Zupok19a].

Reviews: [Brown22]

In addition, ArcA acts as a repressor for <i>rpoS</i> transcription [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16291649">Mika05</a>]. ArcA also activates a few operons encoding proteins involved in fermentative metabolism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8071220">Brondsted94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8892825">Lynch96</a>]. It has been identified as global repressor of carbon oxidation pathways [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. Microarray analyses have identified a large number of genes affected by ArcA and have revealed that the Arc system and the FNR regulatory network overlap to a much greater extent than previously estimated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15699038">Salmon05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14711822">Liu04a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15838044">Perrenoud05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. It has been suggested that the most significant role of ArcA is under microaerobic conditions, while that of FNR is under more strictly anaerobic conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12486057">Alexeeva03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15669087">Levanon05</a>]. For full expression of <i>arcA</i> both FNR and ArcA are required [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8022271">Compan94</a>]. Distinct functional roles for both regulators have been proposed, and it has been shown that there is little direct coregulation of the two [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>].
<p>
ArcA is a response regulator and is activated as a DNA-binding protein by phosphorylation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11527965">Jeon01</a>]. The cognate sensor kinase ArcB is membrane associated and has three cytoplasmic domains; a transmitter, a receiver, and a phosphotransfer (HPt) domain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7957084">Ishige94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1597416">Iuchi92a</a>]. Under anaerobic conditions ArcA is phosphorylated in a phosphorelay reaction that involves phosphotransfer from the autophosphorylated transmitter domain of ArcB to the receiver and Hpt domain of ArcB and finally to the receiver domain of ArcA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10851007">Kwon00c</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8825099">Tsuzuki95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9286997">Georgellis97</a>]. Autophosphorylation of ArcB is stimulated by effectors such as d-lactate, pyruvate, and acetate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10585483">Georgellis99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10585483">Georgellis99</a>]. Under aerobic conditions, the autokinase activity of ArcB is inhibited by quinone electron carriers [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11423658">Georgellis01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15326287">Malpica04</a>], and unphosphorylated ArcB promotes the dephosphorylation of ArcA-P by a reverse phosphorelay reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9830034">Georgellis98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15838055">PenaSandoval05</a>]. It has been suggested that ArcA may also be subject to cross-regulation by other, unknown sensor kinases [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16291649">Mika05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12366850">Oshima02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17213678">Kato07a</a>]. Z nucleotides [ZMP (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide-1-beta-D-ribofuranosyl 5-monophosphate) and/or ZTP (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide-1-beta-D-ribofuranosyl 5-triphosphate)] can act as direct phosphodonors to ArcA <i>in vivo</i>, activating it in an ArcB-independent manner [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33318202">VazquezCiros20</a>].
<p>
ArcA is a member of the OmpR/PhoB subfamily of response regulators and consists of an N-terminal receiver domain and a C-terminal helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain  [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9205844">Mizuno97</a>]. The crystal structures of the receiver domain of ArcA in the presence and absence of the phosphoryl analog BeF<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> have been solved [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15876365">ToroRoman05a</a>]. In the crystal structures, the receiver domain forms a symmetric dimer.
<p>
ArcA appears to be S-nitrosylated on Cys173 in planktonic cells under aerobic growth conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33850153">Barraud21</a>].
<p>
Weight matrices for the DNA-binding site for ArcA-P have been obtained. The proposed binding site consists of 15 bp with a direct spaced repeat [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15728117">Favorov05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10216875">McGuire99</a>]. It has been suggested that multimerization, induced by phosphorylation, is a prerequisite for binding [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11527965">Jeon01</a>]. ArcA represses transcription by directly binding to the promoter or by binding to sites overlapping an activator-binding site [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16849788">Cho06a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15252051">Jeong04b</a>]. As an activator, it  appears to act as part of a nucleoprotein complex. For activation of <i>pfl</i>, a functional interaction between the ArcA and Fnr protein has been suggested [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1592804">Sawers92</a>]. For expression of <i>cydAB</i>, it has been shown that ArcA-P antagonizes H-NS [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11123679">Govantes00</a>]. At the R1 P<sub>Y</sub> promoter, ArcA acts in conjunction with TraJ. ArcA represses and activates transcription solely by binding DNA, and it activates only indirectly when its binding interferes with the binding and repression of another transcriptional repressor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. The majority of ArcA-binding sites overlap the &sigma;<sup>70</sup> promoter recognition elements [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>].
<p>
ArcA is not an essential protein [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32108145">Miyake20</a>]. Under glucose-abundant conditions, the double mutant of <i>iclR arcA</i> causes an increase in biomass yield (47%) and reduction of acetate (70%) and CO<sub>2</sub> (16%) production. Under glucose-limited conditions, this double mutant exhibits an increase of biomass of only 13% [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21481254">Waegeman11</a>]. On the other hand, in an <i>arcA</i> mutant, the TCA cycle flux was increased 4.4 times above that of the wild type in the presence of nitrates, and the intracellular ATP/ADP ratio increased approximately 2-fold above that of the wild-type strain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22790675">Toya12</a>].
<p>
An exhaustive analysis of the ArcA response regulator was carried out, based on different experimental methodologies, High-throughputs (ChIP-chip and ChIP-seq), bioinformatic analysis, DNase I footprinting, and gene expression profiling, and the results showed that ArcA is a global repressor of carbon oxidation pathways [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. ArcA-P directly regulates the expression of 85 operons under anaerobic growth conditions, where 74 operons are repressed and 11 are activated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. The proportion of phosphorylated ArcA is increased in aerobic conditions and the presence of carbon monoxide (CO) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26907100">Wareham16</a>]. It was shown that most ArcA-binding sites contain additional direct repeat (DR) elements as well as the two required for binding an ArcA dimer, and this finding provided a  novel insight into how ArcA accomplishes global regulation of gene expression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. More than 50% of the sites have additional DR elements, and the majority of ArcA-binding sites contain three to five DR elements, predominantly at a CTC spacing of 11 bp [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. The variations in the number, spacing, location, and predicted strength of DR elements within the chromosomal ArcA-binding regions suggest plasticity in the architecture of ArcA-binding sites for either repressed or activated operons [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>].
<p>
The growth [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28573283">Kargeti17</a>] and the net final biomass produced in an <i>arcA</i> single-deletion mutants  growing under anaerobic fermentation conditions were affected relative to responses of the wild-type strain (<i>Escherichia coli</i> strain BW25113) grown in the same conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28573283">Kargeti17</a>]. <i>arcA</i> deletion increased expression of genes involved in acetate assimilation and uptake and also genes involved in the TCA cycle [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29193870">Veeravalli18</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. The mutant also caused decreased nucleotide synthesis, decreased glucose and ammonia uptake rates, and enhanced nitrogen transport and accumulation of amino acids and their precursors, as well as derepression of alternate carbon metabolic proteins [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. The activities of some transcription factors appear to be enhanced (ArgR, NtrC, NrdR) in the arcA mutant, whereas others are diminished (PuuR) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29748694">Kargeti18</a>] et al. reported a relative increase in glucose uptake rate above that required for the observed growth rate in an arcA mutant. In addition, higher ATP synthesis and redox balance rates were reported relative to the observed growth rate and biomass yield in the mutant [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29748694">Kargeti18</a>].
<p>
ArcA promotes dehydration tolerance, both independently and through ArcZ or RpoS [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29457688">Chen18c</a>].
<p>
The accumulation of the protein ArcA is decreased during iron-limiting conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31235512">Zupok19</a>]. A negative correlation between cellular growth and the copy number of the proteins ArcA has been reported [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35694815">Parisutham22</a>].
<p>
ArcA is a flux sensor for the oxygen consumption rate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32383263">Nochino20</a>].
<p>
Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of ArcA appears to increase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33731833">Deter21</a>].
<p>
Deletion of <i>arcA</i> and <i>gutM</i> under three different antibiotics, cefixime, ciprofloxacin, and chloramphenicol, significantly suppressed resistance evolution, which was not caused by epistatic interactions with mutations known to confer drug resistance [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32144279">Horinouchi20</a>].
<p>
When cells are grown in acetate as a carbon source, the knockout mutants of <i>arcA</i> and <i>fis</i> show an improved growth rate and enhanced acetate uptake [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35416487">Jindal22</a>]. This is a consequence of the reprogramming of the carbon metabolic flux generated by the mutants [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35416487">Jindal22</a>].
<p>
A review of the regulation of molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis and molybdoenzyme gene expression via molybdenum and iron by FNR, NarXL/QP, Fur, and ArcA has been published [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31517366">Zupok19a</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35442087">Brown22</a>]</comment>

slots.text:
Nac, "Nitrogen assimilation control," regulates, without a coeffector, genes involved in nitrogen metabolism under nitrogen-limiting conditions [Muse98].

The genes regulated by Nac are transcribed by RNA polymerase σ70. These genes are coupled to the nitrogen regulatory (Ntr) system, which is σ54 dependent, through Nac, whose transcription is activated by NtrC [Muse98]. Using DNA microarray analyses, it was shown that Nac could affect the expression of 25 genes [Zimmer00]. This transcriptional regulator is negatively autoregulated [Muse98] and is expressed under nitrogen-limiting conditions [Camarena98].

Nac belongs to the LysR family [Muse98] and features a helix-turn-helix motif located close to the N terminus [Muse99]. In contrast with most LysR family members, which are transcribed divergently from the gene they regulate, nac is distant on the genome from its regulated genes [Muse98].

In Klebsiella pneumoniae, Nac functions as a dimer, and for some sites it can bind as a tetramer; it recognizes long and short sites in the absence of a coeffector [Rosario10].

High concentrations of Nac appear to stop cellular growth [Parisutham22].

Review: [Switzer18].

<comment datatype="string">Nac, "<b>N</b>itrogen <b>a</b>ssimilation <b>c</b>ontrol," regulates, without a coeffector, genes involved in nitrogen metabolism under  nitrogen-limiting conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9495755">Muse98</a>].
<p>
The genes regulated by Nac are transcribed by RNA polymerase &sigma;<sup>70</sup>. These genes are coupled to the nitrogen regulatory (Ntr) system, which is &sigma;<sup>54</sup> dependent, through Nac, whose transcription is activated by NtrC [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9495755">Muse98</a>]. Using DNA microarray analyses, it was shown that Nac could affect the expression of 25 genes [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11121068">Zimmer00</a>]. This transcriptional regulator is negatively autoregulated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9495755">Muse98</a>] and is expressed under nitrogen-limiting conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9785451">Camarena98</a>].
<p>
Nac belongs to the LysR family [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9495755">Muse98</a>] and features a helix-turn-helix motif located close to the N terminus [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9922258">Muse99</a>]. In contrast with most LysR family members, which are transcribed divergently from the gene they regulate, <i>nac</i> is distant on the genome from its regulated genes [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9495755">Muse98</a>].
<p>
In <i>Klebsiella pneumoniae</i>, Nac functions as a dimer, and for some sites it can bind as a tetramer; it recognizes long and short sites in the absence of a coeffector [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20363946">Rosario10</a>].
<p>
High concentrations of Nac appear to stop cellular growth [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35694815">Parisutham22</a>].
<p>
Review: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30514772">Switzer18</a>].</comment>

slots.text:
PhoB is a dual transcription regulator that activates expression of the Pho regulon in response to environmental Pi. The Pho regulon includes operons and genes whose products are involved in phosphorus uptake and metabolism [Wanner93, VanBogelen96, Baek06]. Expression of the periplasmic binding proteins for peptide transport, OppA and DppA, is repressed by PhoB [Smith92a].

PhoB is a response regulator and belongs to the two-component system PhoR/PhoB. Under phosphate limitation conditions the inner membrane sensor kinase PhoR autophosphorylates. Subsequent transfer of the phosphate group to PhoB results in activation of PhoB [Makino89]. When phosphate is in excess, autophosphorylation of PhoR is inhibited and PhoB-P is dephosphorylated. This negative regulation requires in addition to PhoR an intact Pst system and PhoU [Wanner96a]. In the absence of PhoR, cross-regulation of PhoB by CreC or acetyl phosphate results in phosphorylation of PhoB in response to carbon sources [Wanner92a, Amemura90].

PhoB consists of two functional domains, the N-terminal receiver domain, which is phosphorylated, and the C-terminal output domain, which binds to DNA and interacts with the σ70-subunit of RNA polymerase to activate transcription [Makino96, Makino93]. The crystal structure of a subcomplex, which includes the σ4 domain of the σ70 factor fused with the RNAP β-subunit flap tip helix, shows that the σ4 domain is recruited to the pho box promoters by PhoB and reorients the σ4 domain with respect to its binding site [Blanco11]. The output domain belongs to the winged helix-turn-helix family of transcription factors [MartinezHackert97a]. Its activity is silenced by the receiver domain, and phosphorylation relieves inhibition [Ellison00]. The 3D structure has been solved for the receiver domain [Sola99] and two constitutively active mutants of this domain [ArribasBosacoma07], as well as that for the output domain [MartinezHackert97]. Aspartic acid 196 (D196) and arginine 219 (R219), located in the C-terminal DNA-binding domain minor groove, are necessary for the binding process for the PhoB transcriptional regulator [Ritzefeld11]. Based on biochemical analysis, a positive cooperative binding mechanism of PhoBDBD (DNA-binding domain) to its cognate DNA sequence and a decisive contribution of dimerization to the complex stability were demonstrated [Ritzefeld13].

PhoB binds to the Pho box, which has been described as two direct 11-bp repeats consisting of successive 7-bp direct repeats followed by an A/T-rich region of 4 bp, situated 10 bp upstream of the -10 region [Makino88, Blanco02, Makino86]. The pho promoters contain functional -10 sequences but lack the consensus -35 sequence [Kimura89a].

The 3D structures of the receiver domain in the absence and presence of the phosphoryl analog beryllium fluoride [Bachhawat05, Sola99], and of two constitutively active mutants of this domain [ArribasBosacoma07], have been solved. The data reveal that the active and inactive receiver domains dimerize in two different orientations relative to each other. Also, the 3D structures of the output domain without DNA [Okamura00] and in complex with its target DNA have been solved [Blanco02]. These data reveal that the output domains bind in a novel tandem arrangement, in which several monomers bind head to tail to successive 11-bp direct repeat sequences, coating one face of the double helix [Blanco02]. In addition, a hybrid protein, in which the receiver domain has been replaced by a leucine zipper, is active in vivo as a transcriptional activator [Mack09].

Taken together these data suggest that PhoB is activated through an intermolecular mechanism. In unphosphorylated PhoB the output domains are constrained. Phosphorylation changes the relative orientation of the subunits to each other, such that orientational constraints between the output domains are lost, allowing the tandem head-to-tail orientation for the active conformation [Bachhawat05, Mack09, Blanco02].

PhoB is not an essential protein, but when OmpR is removed from the cell along with PhoB or PhoP, cellular adaptative growth is disrupted. However, growth was not affected in a triple knockout involving ompR, phoB, and phoP [Miyake20].

<comment datatype="string">PhoB is a dual transcription regulator that activates expression of the Pho regulon in response to environmental P<sub>i</sub>. The Pho regulon includes operons and genes whose products are involved in phosphorus uptake and metabolism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8432742">Wanner93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8755861">VanBogelen96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17020555">Baek06</a>]. Expression of the periplasmic binding proteins for peptide transport, OppA and DppA, is repressed by PhoB [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1478454">Smith92a</a>].  
<p>
PhoB is a response regulator and belongs to the two-component system PhoR/PhoB. Under phosphate limitation conditions the inner membrane sensor kinase PhoR autophosphorylates. Subsequent transfer of the phosphate group to PhoB results in activation of PhoB [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2693738">Makino89</a>]. When phosphate is in excess, autophosphorylation of PhoR is inhibited and PhoB-P is dephosphorylated. This negative regulation requires in addition to PhoR an intact Pst system and PhoU [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8691745">Wanner96a</a>]. In the absence of PhoR, cross-regulation of PhoB by CreC or acetyl phosphate results in phosphorylation of PhoB in response to carbon sources [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1551836">Wanner92a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2228961">Amemura90</a>]. 
<p>
PhoB consists of two functional domains, the N-terminal receiver domain, which is phosphorylated, and the C-terminal output domain, which binds to DNA and interacts with the &sigma;<sup>70</sup>-subunit of RNA polymerase to activate transcription [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8648643">Makino96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8422984">Makino93</a>]. The crystal structure of a subcomplex, which includes the &sigma;<sub>4</sub> domain of the &sigma;<sup>70</sup> factor fused with the RNAP &beta;-subunit flap tip helix, shows that the &sigma;<sub>4</sub> domain is recruited to the <i>pho</i> box promoters by PhoB and reorients the &sigma;<sub>4</sub> domain with respect to its binding site [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21829166">Blanco11</a>]. The output domain belongs to the winged helix-turn-helix family of transcription factors [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9199401">MartinezHackert97a</a>]. Its activity is silenced by the receiver domain, and phosphorylation relieves inhibition [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11073900">Ellison00</a>]. The 3D structure has been solved for the receiver domain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9878437">Sola99</a>] and two constitutively active mutants of this domain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17182055">ArribasBosacoma07</a>], as well as that for the output domain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9016718">MartinezHackert97</a>]. Aspartic acid 196 (D196) and arginine 219 (R219), located in the C-terminal DNA-binding domain minor groove, are necessary for the binding process for the PhoB transcriptional regulator [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21912786">Ritzefeld11</a>]. Based on biochemical analysis, a positive cooperative binding mechanism of PhoB<sup>DBD</sup> (DNA-binding domain) to its cognate DNA sequence and a decisive contribution of dimerization to the complex stability were demonstrated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24199636">Ritzefeld13</a>].
<p>
PhoB binds to the Pho box, which has been described as two direct 11-bp repeats consisting of successive 7-bp direct repeats followed by an A/T-rich region of 4 bp, situated 10 bp upstream of the -10 region [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3054125">Makino88</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12015152">Blanco02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3537313">Makino86</a>]. The <i>pho</i> promoters contain functional  -10 sequences but lack the consensus  -35 sequence [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2651888">Kimura89a</a>].
<p>
The 3D structures of the receiver domain in the absence and presence of the phosphoryl analog beryllium fluoride [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16154092">Bachhawat05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9878437">Sola99</a>], and of two constitutively active mutants of this domain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17182055">ArribasBosacoma07</a>], have been solved. The data reveal that the active and inactive receiver domains dimerize in two different orientations relative to each other. Also, the 3D structures of the output domain without DNA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10653699">Okamura00</a>] and in complex with its target DNA have been solved [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12015152">Blanco02</a>]. These data reveal that the output domains bind in a novel tandem arrangement, in which several monomers bind head to tail to successive 11-bp direct repeat sequences, coating one face of the double helix [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12015152">Blanco02</a>]. In addition, a hybrid protein, in which the receiver domain has been replaced by a leucine zipper, is active <i>in vivo</i> as a transcriptional activator [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19371748">Mack09</a>]. 
<p>
Taken together these data suggest that PhoB is activated through an intermolecular mechanism. In unphosphorylated PhoB the output domains are constrained. Phosphorylation changes the relative orientation of the subunits to each other, such that orientational constraints between the output domains are lost, allowing the tandem head-to-tail orientation for the active conformation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16154092">Bachhawat05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19371748">Mack09</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12015152">Blanco02</a>].
<p>
PhoB is not an essential protein, but when OmpR is removed from the cell along with PhoB or PhoP, cellular adaptative growth is disrupted. However, growth was not affected in a triple knockout involving <i>ompR</i>, <i>phoB</i>, and <i>phoP</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32108145">Miyake20</a>].

slots.text:
PhoB is a dual transcription regulator that activates expression of the Pho regulon in response to environmental Pi. The Pho regulon includes operons and genes whose products are involved in phosphorus uptake and metabolism [Wanner93, VanBogelen96, Baek06]. Expression of the periplasmic binding proteins for peptide transport, OppA and DppA, is repressed by PhoB [Smith92a]. In a proteomic analysis under phosphate-limiting conditions, it was found that up to 400 proteins are differentially expressed [VanBogelen96]. PhoB is also involved in bacterial virulence of pathogenic Escherichia coli [Crepin11]. PhoB also regulates genes involved in the stimulation of cell persister resuscitation [Song21a].

PhoB is a response regulator and belongs to the two-component system PhoR/PhoB. Under phosphate-limited conditions, the inner membrane sensor kinase PhoR autophosphorylates. Subsequent transfer of the phosphate group to PhoB results in activation of PhoB [Makino89]. When phosphate is in excess, autophosphorylation of PhoR is inhibited and PhoB-P is dephosphorylated. Autoregulation of PhoB/PhoR expression serves as a mechanism for cells to achieve respective optimal densities and fitness under these conditions [Gao13c]. This negative regulation requires in addition to PhoR an intact Pst system and PhoU [Wanner96a]. In the absence of PhoR, cross-regulation of PhoB by CreC or acetyl phosphate results in phosphorylation of PhoB in response to carbon sources [Wanner92a, Amemura90]. A heterodimer formed between a phosphorylated monomer and an unphosphorylated monomer of PhoB plays an important role in PhoB autophosphorylation kinetics [CreagerAllen13].

PhoB consists of two functional domains, the N-terminal receiver domain, which is phosphorylated, and the C-terminal output domain, which binds to DNA and interacts with the σ70 subunit of RNA polymerase to activate transcription [Makino96, Makino93]. The output domain belongs to the winged helix-turn-helix family of transcription factors [MartinezHackert97a]. Its activity is silenced by the receiver domain, and phosphorylation relieves inhibition [Ellison00]. The 3D structure of the receiver domain [Sola99] and of two constitutively active mutants of this domain [ArribasBosacoma07] and the 3D structure of the output domain have been solved [MartinezHackert97]. By using motif binding geometries (MBG), a structural model of the PhoB dimer in the transcription initiation complex PhoB/RNAP/σ factor/DNA has been developed [Tung12].

PhoB binds to the Pho box, the structure of a PhoB-DNA complex, revealing that sequence changes within the 4-bp region can alter the binding affinity without changing the major groove-contacting TGTCA tract that is important for binding specificity. Sequences are less conserved within this 4-bp region than in the rest of the 18-bp region [Gao15a]. The 18-bp region has been described as two direct 11-bp repeats consisting of successive 7-bp direct repeats followed by an A/T-rich region of 4 bp, situated 10 bp upstream of the -10 region [Makino88, Blanco02, Makino86]. The pho promoters contain functional -10 sequences but lack the consensus -35 sequence [Kimura89a].

The 3D structure of the PhoB effector domain in complex with its target DNA sequence reveals a novel tandem arrangement in which several monomers bind head to tail to successive 11-bp direct repeat sequences, coating one face of the double helix [Blanco02, Bachhawat05].

Based on DNA microarray analysis, it has been shown that PhoBR and PhoB are responsible for upregulation of phosphonate and glycerol phosphate metabolism and the high-affinity phosphate transport system, respectively, thus showing the complex regulation by the PhoR-PhoB two-component regulatory system [Baek07a]. The expression timing of PhoB regulation and the temporal hierarchy are related, as the genes involved in direct Pi uptake contain high-affinity sites and are transcribed earlier than genes involved in phosphorus scavenging [Gao15a]. Although PhoB is activated under Pi limitation, it can also be activated under nonlimiting Pi conditions [GrilloPuertas16].

PhoB is involved in the inhibition of biofilm formation that is triggered by fluctuations in poly(P) levels during the stationary phase [GrilloPuertas16].

Based on results of a transcription reporter assay and in vivo phosphorylation analysis, the shutoff response for the PhoR-PhoB system was determined [Gao17b]. These comprehensive analyses revealed the impact of phosphatase activity on shutoff kinetics. The ratio of the phosphatase rate to the nonspecific phosphorylation rate correlated with TCS expression levels and the ratio of activity of the RR (PhoB response regulator) to that of the HK (histidine kinase), which may contribute to the great diversity of enzyme levels and the activities observed in different TCSs [Gao17b].

The memory of the PhoB-PhoR two-component system (TCS) was used to study how cells cope with the recurrence of Pi starvation via a TCS. Memory prior Pi starvation can exert distinct effects through two regulatory pathways, TCS signaling and the stress response [Gao17c]. The crystal structures for inactivated and BeF3-activated PhoBN (N-terminal receiver domain) were solved by using X-ray at 2.4 and 1.9 A resolution, respectively [Kou18]. The backbone assignment of a PhoBNF20D mutant has been determined using NMR spectroscopy, and this information could be useful for studying the structure and dynamics of the PhoB receiver domain and its mechanism of phosphorylation in TCSs [Kou18]. Based on NMR spectroscopy, the apo form of the N-terminal receiver domain (PhoBN) in solution was determined [Kou18a]. In addition, it was shown via concentration dilution experiments and backbone relaxation parameters that PhoBN exists in equilibrium between monomer and dimer states. Finally, paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (PRE) measurements showed that the dimer of apo PhoBN forms several transient dimer interfaces in solution [Kou18a].

Based on wild-type and recombinant cells cultivated in two different substrates (lactose and glycerol), the effect of phosphate-starved response (PSR) stimuli was investigated. Gene expression analysis showed that under PSR conditions, selected genes (gapA, pykF, ppsA, icdA) in the glycolysis and pentose phosphate pathways (zwf, gnd, talB, tktA) were up-regulated, whereas other genes in lactose (lacY, lacA) and acetate (ackA, pta) metabolism pathways were down-regulated. It was also demonstrated that Cra, CRP transcription factors, and the PhoBR two-component signal transduction system are involved in the regulation of central carbon metabolism [Pandi20].

An NADP phosphatase is thought to take part in the interconversion of NAD and NADP, reversing the activity of NAD kinase [Lundquist71]. There is no gene as yet associated with this hypothetical enzyme.

CysQ exhibits NADP(H) phosphatase activity in vitro, although this is not thought to be the physiological activity of that enzyme [Fukuda07]. Reviewed in [Kawai08].
